summary:
Argentina's Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

Mendoza stands under that national framework, and no Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern for transgender visitors is documented. The province also has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating its own record of anti-trans violence, so the absence of Mendoza data reflects the absence of a counting mechanism rather than an absence of events.

The national framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than repeal. The decree of 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender prisoners. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here. In parallel, the 1 per cent Trans Labor Quota had its hires dismissed and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished in 2024.

National hate-crime recording reached a ten-year record in 2025: the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio counted at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rise of 62 per cent year on year and an average of one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space; beatings were the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, 32 per cent of 2025 incidents occurred inside police stations or prisons, and 43 per cent of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Activists interviewed in Buenos Aires in April 2025 told the Washington Blade that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common under President Javier Milei, and that the position is worse "even more so" in interior provinces without strong reporting infrastructure. Mendoza is an interior province of that kind. The Blade interviews, conducted on 4 and 10 April 2025, included organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, and described the community's situation as chaotic and desperate.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeal court in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration despite the statute remaining in force.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting on trans violence in Argentina is concentrated in Buenos Aires, where national observatories and press outlets are based; provinces are covered through the national aggregate rather than through independent local counting. Visitors to Mendoza should read national figures as the ceiling of what is documented here, not as a Mendoza measurement.

The trend direction is national rather than regional: hate crimes rose 62 per cent between 2024 and 2025 and institutional violence nearly quadrupled over the same period, so a visitor's exposure to state actors carries more documented risk than a generic street-crime framing suggests.

Argentina's position is one of divergence between statute and administration. The recognition statute, marriage equality and provincial anti-discrimination laws remain in place while the anti-discrimination agency, the employment quota and access to care for minors have been removed or restricted by executive measure, a pattern documented across the country rather than originating in Mendoza.
localsOnly:
Provincial residents access legal gender change through Law 26.743 at national registries without surgery, hormones or a court order, and the 1 per cent Trans Labor Quota in public employment has been rendered unenforceable through dismissal of its hires.

Residents lost the federal anti-discrimination complaint route when INADI was abolished in 2024; recourse now runs through provincial anti-discrimination provisions and the courts, and no Mendoza provincial enforcement series for those provisions is documented.

Minors resident in the province are barred from gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment by the decree of 5 February 2025, and transgender detainees are subject to the separate decree governing their placement in prisons.

The Decazo-era contraction of public funding, the closures of gender-identity services and the dismissal of quota hires affect residents' everyday access to care and work, conditions that also shape the street-level environment trans residents navigate with police.
outOfScopeNotes:
The litigation challenging the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources available here: legal experts petitioned for judicial intervention and no outcome is recorded.

No Mendoza-specific incident count, police-encounter record or provincial hate-crime tally exists in the inventory; the province's position is inferred from national figures plus the activists' statement that interior provinces have weaker reporting infrastructure. Whether Mendoza maintains any unpublicised provincial counting mechanism is not sourced either way.

The Outright International overview of 12 March 2026 gives negative ratings on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration without the inventory stating the criteria behind each rating or whether any subnational variation applies to Mendoza.

The 227 recorded hate crimes for 2025 are national and are not disaggregated by province in the sources, so no share attributable to Mendoza can be stated.
